name: Didaskolos
personality: Gentle and encouraging, he speaks in simple, repeatable phrases and celebrates small successes. Calm under pressure, he notices confusion quickly and rephrases with a smile. Playful and curious, he turns lessons into games that feel like discoveries.
backstory: Raised in the same forest, he learned Greek rhythms from his grandmother’s songs and grew to love teaching younger neighbors. He apprenticed with the village schoolkeeper, collecting stories and simple phrases that children could act out. When the school opened under the pines, he chose to stay close to home so every creature could learn together. He still gathers pebbles, leaves, and little signs from walks to use as hands-on tools.
appearance: A modest-sized tawny owl with a cream-speckled breast and soft brown wings, he wears a sky-blue knit cardigan with oval elbow patches and wooden buttons. Thin wire-rim spectacles hang from a cord at his chest, and a woven reed satchel rests against his hip, often bulging with papyrus scraps and a wax tablet. His yellow talons show a tiny nick on the right foot, and he sometimes carries a smooth twig as a pointer. Scenes are drawn from a child’s eye level, so his cardigan hem, satchel, and talons are usually in frame while his head sits out of view.
strengths: He explains concepts with clear, high-frequency phrases and purposeful repetition.
He reads the room quickly and adjusts pace and examples to match attention and mood.
He builds confidence through gentle praise and small, achievable tasks.
He turns everyday objects into memorable teaching aids.
weaknesses: He can over-explain, slowing the group when excitement is high.
Without his spectacles, he misses small details on pages or slates.
His voice is soft and can be lost in windy outdoor lessons.
key_objects: Wire-rim spectacles on a cord that he fingers when thinking.
A woven reed satchel filled with papyrus scraps, a wax tablet, and a reed stylus.
A smooth twig pointer used to tap letters, maps, and game pieces.
relationships: Mentor to the forest’s young animals, especially the siblings who speak Greek at home.
Collaborates with caregivers to send home simple songs and phrases for practice.
Respected by village helpers who lend materials for his hands-on lessons.
